title: Polynomial-time tractability testing for core crisp CSP languages
formal: Is there one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite crisp constraint language \(\Gamma\) over an explicitly given finite domain D and promised that \(\Gamma\) is a core, decides whether \(\Gamma\) admits an idempotent Siggers polymorphism? Equivalently on the core promise, decide whether \(\Gamma\) is solvable in the algebraic sense of the finite-domain CSP dichotomy. The polynomial must be uniform in the entire input, including |D|, the number of relations, their arities and their listed tuples; neither a polymorphism nor a tractability certificate is supplied.
context:
Testing tractability for arbitrary crisp languages is NP-complete, and testing core status is itself difficult. The question assumes core status from the start; neither hardness result alone classifies the promised problem.

Theorem 16 gives a polynomial algorithm for the relevant binary symmetric fractional polymorphism of a core finite-valued language. Crisp relations use forbidden assignments with infinite cost, so that finite-valued theorem does not provide this Siggers test.

The source states that a uniform polynomial-time solver for all solvable core crisp languages would imply the desired test. The fixed-template dichotomy alone does not give a polynomial uniform in the varying input language.

Bodirsky and Weiß explicitly distinguish idempotent Siggers testing from the unrestricted NP-complete metaproblem and note the equivalence under the core promise. Their results on coset-generating and promise metaproblems do not give the general Siggers test.
why: Would make the finite-domain CSP tractability criterion efficiently recognizable when the core is already given, connecting the structural dichotomy to algorithms whose template also varies as input.
status_note: Checked the source’s encoding, core definition and algebraic solvability convention, its complete April 2019 version, and the explicit ICALP 2026 discussion following Theorem 4. Broader searches through 12 September 2026 found no polynomial core-crisp Siggers test or matching promised-core hardness result. The 2026 primary source directly supports continued openness; search is not exhaustive.

references.title: Testing the Complexity of a Valued CSP Language
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 8; PDF page 8

definitions: A crisp language is a finite set \(\Gamma\) of relations \(R\subseteq D\)ʳ of possibly different finite arities on a finite nonempty explicitly listed domain D. Each relation is given by its arity and a list of its allowed tuples; unlisted tuples are forbidden. This is equivalent to a cost function with value 0 on allowed tuples and +∞ elsewhere. The input size N includes D, relation delimiters, arities and the binary encodings of all listed entries. There is no fixed bound on |D| or arity imposed outside the input. An m-ary operation \(g:D^{m}\to D\) preserves an r-ary relation R if, for every m tuples \(a^{1},\ldots ,a^{m}\in R\), the coordinatewise tuple \((g(a^{1}_{1},\ldots ,a^{m}_{1}),\ldots ,g(a^{1}_{r},\ldots ,a^{m}_{r}))\) lies in R. A polymorphism of \(\Gamma\) preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\). The language is a core if every unary polymorphism \(u:D\to D\) is bijective; for a finite relational structure such a map is an automorphism. Core status is promised rather than something the requested algorithm must verify. An idempotent Siggers polymorphism is a four-ary operation \(s:D^{4}\to D\) that preserves every relation and satisfies \(s(x,x,x,x)=x\) for all \(x\in D\) and \(s(r,a,r,e)=s(a,r,e,a)\) for every \(r,a,e\in D\). On a core, existence of a Siggers operation without the idempotence identity is equivalent to existence of an idempotent one. An ordinary \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma )\) instance has variables and constraints requiring selected variable tuples to belong to relations of \(\Gamma\); it asks for a satisfying assignment from D. In the source’s terminology, solvable means satisfying the dichotomy’s polymorphism criterion. Such languages have polynomial-time CSP algorithms when \(\Gamma\) is fixed; failure of the criterion gives NP-hardness. The present target tests that algebraic criterion and does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in order to define its yes/no answers. The requested machine must halt in \(N^{O(1)}\) time on all inputs and be correct on every input satisfying the core promise. Its behavior on non-core inputs is unrestricted. The task only asks to decide existence, not to output the operation table, although a four-ary table has |\(D|^{4}\) entries and gives a polynomial-size, polynomially checkable existence certificate.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with one polynomial running-time bound in N that accepts exactly the promised core languages having such a polymorphism, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness statement requires the core promise to be respected. Testing whether the input is a core, classifying languages without that promise, or solving CSP instances for one fixed tractable template does not settle this meta-decision problem.
